claims.claim: All Herodotus quotations are verbatim from G. C. Macaulay's translation: vol. I (Gutenberg #2707, prepared from the 1890 Macmillan edition) and vol. II (Gutenberg #2456, prepared from the 1914 third edition). Macaulay died 1915. Headers checked.

Macaulay's footnote numbers were removed by script (28 of them, listed by extract.py: e.g. 'to the end that 1 neither', 'sent away 228 by Leonidas'); no word changed. Chapter numbers at paragraph starts are kept.
Thucydides quotations verbatim from Richard Crawley (1874; d. 1893), Gutenberg #7142; header checked. No footnote markers in the passages used.

Dionysius' letter (Eusebius, Church History VII.22.2–3, 6–10) verbatim from A. C. McGiffert, NPNF II.1 (1890; d. 1933), via New Advent 250107. New Advent's section numbers and its inserted reference 'Exodus 12:30' were removed; the cut of §4–5 is marked '…'.
Augustine, City of God IV.4 verbatim from Marcus Dods (d. 1909), NPNF I.2 (1887), New Advent 120104. Note: Dods' text reads 'while you who does it with a great fleet' (sic), kept verbatim.
Herodotus was born c. 484 BC at Halicarnassus (Bodrum), lived at Thurii, died c. 425 BC.
claims.source: OCD (4th ed.) s.v. Herodotus; Marincola, Greek Historians (2001)

claims.claim: Cicero called Herodotus 'the father of history' and mentioned his 'countless stories' (innumerabiles fabulae) in the same sentence.
Plutarch called Herodotus philobarbaros, 'friend of barbarians'.
claims.source: Plutarch, On the Malice of Herodotus 12 (857a)

claims.claim: Hecataeus fragment: 'I write what seems to me to be true, for the stories of the Greeks are many and absurd' (our translation).
Cyrus took Sardis c. 547 BC and Babylon in 539 BC; Persian Empire founded c. 550 BC; Darius reigned 522–486; Xerxes 486–465.
claims.source: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002); Nabonidus Chronicle

claims.claim: Athens had about 30,000 citizens (Herodotus' figure).
Herodotus measured/described the pyramids (II.124–127), Croesus' gifts at Delphi (I.50–51), gold-digging ants (III.102).
Lydians first to strike gold and silver coins.
Solon's laws c. 594 BC; ten years' travel.
Plutarch knew the chronological objection to the Solon–Croesus meeting and kept the story.
Delphi's reply: Croesus paid for his fifth ancestor's crime and should have asked which empire; 'let him pronounce himself to be the cause'.
Herodotus I.34: 'a great retribution from God came upon Croesus, probably because he judged himself to be the happiest of all men'.
Nabonidus Chronicle, year 9 (547 BC): Cyrus marched to a land (name damaged, often read Lydia) and killed its king.
claims.source: British Museum; Grayson, Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles (1975), Chronicle 7

claims.claim: Bacchylides, Ode 3 (468 BC): Apollo carries Croesus to the Hyperboreans.
Attic red-figure amphora by Myson, c. 500–490 BC, Louvre G 197, shows Croesus on the pyre.
Aeschylus' Persians (472 BC) is the oldest surviving tragedy.
Xerxes whipped the Hellespont.
Divine Providence passage.
Aristotle discusses Solon's saying and Priam.
Marathon: 6,400 Persians and 192 Athenians dead.
Demaratus deposed c. 491 BC.
Thermopylae: Leonidas kept 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, 400 Thebans.
Herodotus' total for Xerxes' force: 5,283,220 men.
Modern estimates of Xerxes' army c. 100,000–300,000.
Pausanias saw a list of the 300 at Sparta.
Marinatos excavated Kolonos hill in 1939 and found Persian arrowheads.
Serpent Column (Delphi, now Istanbul Hippodrome) lists the cities that fought.
claims.source: Herodotus IX.81; Meiggs and Lewis, GHI 27

claims.claim: Behistun names five of Herodotus' six fellow conspirators.
Scythian burials match IV.71–72.
claims.source: Rolle, The World of the Scythians (1989)

claims.claim: Herodotus V.78 on Athens' freedom: quoted verbatim from Macaulay.
Herodotus I.136: Persian boys taught 'in riding, in shooting, and in speaking the truth'.
Spartans' annual declaration of war on the helots.
J. S. Mill: Marathon more important to English history than Hastings.
claims.source: Mill, review of Grote, Edinburgh Review 84 (1846)

claims.claim: Fehling (1971) and Pritchett (1993) on Herodotus' sources.
Thucydides: born c. 460, caught plague (II.48), exiled after Amphipolis 424 (IV.104–107; V.26), links to Thracian gold mines (IV.105), history breaks off 411 BC.
V.26 'being of an age to comprehend events' (Crawley).
Treaty of 421 copied (V.18–19); 'fear, honour and interest' (I.76).
Athenian tribute reassessment 425 BC (IG I³ 71) lists Melos at 15 talents.
claims.source: IG I³ 71; Meiggs and Lewis GHI 69

claims.claim: Walls of Athens pulled down to flute music.
Corinth and Thebes proposed destroying Athens in 404; Sparta refused.
Cornford (1907), Hunter (1973), Hornblower (1987, 1991–2008), de Romilly (1947), Kagan, Allison (2017: 16 cases, 12 wars).
Hobbes translated Thucydides 1629; Leviathan ch. 13 quotation verbatim from Gutenberg #3207.
Thrasymachus: 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger' (Jowett).
Plague: Thucydides III.87 gives 4,400 hoplites and 300 cavalry dead and 'a number of the multitude that was never ascertained'.
Kerameikos mass grave found 1994–95, c. 150 bodies; Papagrigorakis et al. (2006) typhoid; Shapiro, Rambaut and Gilbert (2006) reply.
II.37 'that code which, although unwritten...'; II.64 'the only point indeed at which our calculation has been at fault'; III.82 'Words had to change their ordinary meaning' (Crawley).
Plague of Cyprian 249–262; Dionysius bishop c. 248–264; letter c. 260.
claims.source: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017); Eusebius VII

claims.claim: Julian's letter to Arsacius (362) on Christians feeding pagan poor (paraphrased, not quoted).
Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996), ch. 4.
Luther, Whether One May Flee from a Deadly Plague (1527); Charles Borromeo in the Milan plague of 1576–77.
Procopius' account of the plague of 542 imitates Thucydides.
claims.source: Procopius, Wars II.22–23; Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea (2004)

claims.claim: Melos: 38 ships, c. 3,400 men; Nicias ravaged Melos in 426 (III.91).
Euripides' Trojan Women staged spring 415 BC; link to Melos debated.
Isocrates defends Athens' treatment of Melos.
Callicles' argument (paraphrased) and Xerxes as example.
Machiavelli's advice (paraphrased).
Morgenthau (1948) opposed the Vietnam War on realist grounds; Waltz (1979).
Assyria destroyed Samaria 722 BC; fell 612 BC; Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem 701 BC.
Sicilian expedition: 134 triremes, 5,100 hoplites (VI.43); 'ignorant of its size' (VI.1); Nicias' eclipse delay (VII.50); army c. 40,000 (VII.75).
Prisoners freed for reciting Euripides.
Augustine wrote City of God 413–426 after the sack of 410; pirate story from Cicero, Republic III.24.
Momigliano (1966, 1990), Yerushalmi (1982), Halpern (1988), Van Seters (1983).
Bede (731) names his sources in his preface; Ranke 1824 'wie es eigentlich gewesen'.
Loveday Alexander (1993) on Luke's preface.
Music notes: Tavener wrote Song for Athene in 1993 for Athene Hariades; Lyte wrote Abide with Me in 1847; Bach's B minor Mass not performed complete in his lifetime; Beethoven's Missa Solemnis.
Scripture (Luke 1:1–4; 12:13–21; Isaiah 10:5–15, and verses quoted in lectures) from the WEB via web.py; lecture quotations checked with web.verse.

flags: PLEASE CHECK: the phrase 'father of lies' for Herodotus is attributed loosely to 'later readers'; I found no single ancient source for the exact phrase.
PLEASE CHECK: 'Cleon may have been behind his exile' rests on the late Life of Thucydides by Marcellinus; it is marked 'may'.
PLEASE CHECK: modern estimate that a quarter to a third of Athens died of the plague.
PLEASE CHECK: Xerxes' army estimate 100,000–300,000; ranges vary widely in the literature.
PLEASE CHECK: Solon's dates (fl. c. 594 BC; d. c. 560) and Croesus' accession (c. 560) as stated.
Spec deviation: session 3's compare is Herodotus VII.223–228 (Thermopylae itself) instead of Exodus 14 (which belongs to 'Exodus and the law'); Exodus 14 is pointed back to in the lecture.

Spec deviation: sessions 3 and 4 add new memory pieces (tell-the-spartans, Herodotus VII.228; possession-for-all-time, Thucydides I.22) where the spec said 'none new'. Drop them at review if unwanted; no other journey creates them.
Spec deviation: the spec reads Herodotus VII.44–52; I read VII.44–46 only (Xerxes weeps), since 47–52 (strategy and the Ionians) does not serve the session's question.

Music: the spec had no music for sessions 1–4 and 6; DECISIONS requires music, so I chose song-for-athene, abide-with-me, faure-requiem, mass-in-b-minor and gorecki-3, each with an honest why. Closing: missa-solemnis.

Paintings: sessions 1 and 3 have no painting (no NGA work of the subject). Sessions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 use near subjects (vanitas, a scholar's portrait, a convalescent, Pompeii, Messina), each 'why' saying plainly what the painting really is.

Dionysius' letter is quoted in one sentence in first-christians' lecture; here it is read in full as a comparison text. first-christians comes earlier on the path; the compare 'why' points back to it. Lead agent please confirm this is acceptable under DECISIONS ('passage set in two journeys').
Augustine City of God IV.4 is mentioned in a table row in democracy (not read); here it is read and becomes a memory piece.
Memory luke-12-20: the opening quotation mark of Jesus' story is dropped from the first line; words verbatim WEB.
Read parts use kind 'philosophy' for Herodotus and Thucydides because the app has no 'history' kind.
Gwen John (d. 1939): image is NGA open access, as in the plan.
